Of the unclaimed prize money on "EMERALD MINE 9X", about three-quarters is in wins under $500. The game is a game with most of its money in small, frequent prizes. That is neither good nor bad, only how it was designed. Choose the kind of game that fits the win you want.

If you play "EMERALD MINE 9X" often, bookmark this page. The write-up is updated with each morning's data.
5055.headline: How the prize money is divided

5057.body:
"EASY MONEY" has 412,998 prizes of $2 still unclaimed, which is its most common win. Just below the top prize is the $10,000 prize, with two left. The full count for every prize level is listed below.

The table below shows the full count for "EASY MONEY", with every prize level included.
5057.headline: The prize table, line by line

5059.body:
"THE CASH WHEEL" is past the halfway point of its run, with about a third of its tickets still unsold. Late in a run, a game is worth a look when prizes outlast tickets. Early on, the prize design matters most. Here, the top prizes and the tickets are going at about the same pace.

Everything here about "THE CASH WHEEL" comes from official Florida lottery numbers, current through November 10.
5059.headline: Early stage or late

5060.body:
The most common win left on "FIND THE 7S" is $2. The second biggest prize left is $500, and 47 of those are still unclaimed. The prize table is what defines a scratcher, and this page counts every level of it.

Tomorrow's count on "FIND THE 7S" will be a little different. The game sells every day, and this page keeps track.
5060.headline: A close look at the prizes

5063.body:
One of CA$H IN HAND's top prizes was claimed over a week ago. A player in Florida won $2 million. The game started with four top prizes and now has two top prizes. Nothing bigger can change on a scratcher.

For "CA$H IN HAND" or any game, being late in a run is not automatically good or bad. The same numbers mean different things near the end of a run.

Every line of CA$H IN HAND's prize table below shows today's count, not last month's.
